resources.string: Fehu speaks to resources, value, and the responsibility they bring. Wealth is not only something to enjoy; it is something to manage, protect, and share wisely.
In relationships, Fehu highlights generosity, shared investment, and care that flows in both directions. Give freely without turning affection into transaction.
For purpose, Fehu highlights the skills and opportunities already available to you. Those resources can serve work that feels meaningful, not only productive or profitable.

For security, Fehu highlights the resources that provide stability and support. Careful stewardship helps you maintain what you have, strengthen what is still developing, and use your resources wisely.

For the self, Fehu highlights inner resources such as energy, focus, resilience, and self-worth. Your value is not defined only by external success, but also by the resources you already carry within you.

When reversed, Fehu often reflects fear of scarcity or valuing something only in material terms. Respond to that fear with careful stewardship rather than hoarding, panic, or waste. Reassess what meaningful wealth really means in your life.

In relationships, Fehu reversed can show love becoming transactional, possessive, or withheld out of fear. Care may start to feel like something to earn, owe, control, or keep score of. Give from a place of trust, and address scarcity directly instead of turning affection into leverage.

For purpose, Fehu reversed can show ambition shaped by scarcity, status, or material reward alone. Work can lose meaning when it is driven only by fear, comparison, or the need to prove your worth. Choose goals that create real value, not just visible gain.

For security, Fehu reversed can show fear-driven choices around money or resources. Hoarding, panic, or waste can weaken the safety you are trying to protect. Build security through clear planning and careful stewardship of what you have.

For the self, Fehu reversed can show self-worth being overly tied to external resources, achievements, or possessions. Root your worth more deeply within yourself, rather than in external measures of value.
Uruz is associated with the aurochs, a wild ox symbolizing strength, vitality, and untamed life force.
Uruz may point to strength that comes from instinct, vitality, and grounded courage. This strength is not forced or controlled; it is rooted in resilience and the body’s deeper wisdom.

In relationships, Uruz may point to the courage to show up honestly and with grounded presence. Strength in a relationship is not only intensity or desire; it also shows through authenticity, steadiness, and mutual respect.
For purpose, Uruz may point to work or goals that draw on your natural strength. A direction that genuinely energises you should not depend on force or willpower alone.
For security, Uruz may point to the resilience that helps you stay grounded through uncertainty. Safety is shaped not only by external conditions, but also by the inner strength you can draw on.
For the self, Uruz may point to the strength you feel through your body, instincts, and vitality.

When reversed, Uruz may point to depleted strength, loss of inner drive, or disconnection from your natural power. Stop forcing yourself forward, and rebuild strength by respecting your limits rather than pushing through exhaustion.

In relationships, Uruz reversed may point to one person feeling unsupported, carrying too much, or lacking the strength to show up fully. Strength can also become harmful when it turns into control instead of care.

For purpose, Uruz reversed may point to depleted drive or progress forced through exhaustion. Willpower alone cannot sustain a path that no longer restores your strength or feels meaningful. Recover your energy, then choose a pace and direction you can truly sustain.

For security, Uruz reversed may point to feeling too depleted to protect yourself. Do not mistake constant endurance for resilience. Restore your energy by reducing what drains you, meeting your basic needs consistently, and asking for help before you reach collapse.

For the self, Uruz reversed may point to feeling disconnected from your strength or treating exhaustion as personal failure. Your limits are not proof of weakness; they show where strength needs recovery or wiser use. Rebuild self-trust by recognising when to rest and when to push.
Thurisaz is linked to the thurs, a giant-like force associated with danger, conflict, and raw power.

With Thurisaz, conflict or pressure may need to be met with clear boundaries rather than fear or force. Its protective power lies in knowing what must be defended, what must be confronted, and what should not be crossed.

In relationships, Thurisaz may point to clear boundaries and the courage to face necessary conflict. Honest confrontation may protect the relationship by stopping resentment or crossed boundaries from growing in silence.
For purpose, Thurisaz may point to pressure or demands interfering with the work that matters. Clearer boundaries may be needed to protect the time and effort your work needs.
For security, Thurisaz may point to an exposed area in your safety or stability. Stronger safeguards may be needed to protect your home, resources, or peace.
For the self, Thurisaz may point to the strength needed to face difficult truths. An inner conflict or harmful pattern may need to be met directly.

When reversed, Thurisaz may point to blocked anger, avoided conflict, or force used harmfully. Anger that is suppressed can turn into bitter resentment or harmful outbursts. Choose honest expression with restraint, so conflict can be faced without causing unnecessary harm.

In relationships, Thurisaz reversed may point to unspoken anger, avoided conflict, or anger used to wound. Say what needs to be said with restraint, before resentment turns into punishment or withdrawal.

For purpose, Thurisaz reversed may point to anger shaping your direction. This can look like pursuing a goal to prove someone wrong, pushing for change in ways that cause unnecessary damage, or staying on a path because resentment keeps it alive. Instead, choose actions that serve your values, your healing, and the life you actually want to build.

For security, Thurisaz reversed may show where potential danger is not being recognised or faced directly. Take anger, fear, or unease seriously when they signal that something needs attention. Respond with clear boundaries and timely action, without letting fear or anger make the situation more harmful.

For the self, Thurisaz reversed may point to destructive anger turned against yourself or released without control. This can look like harsh self-criticism, silent resentment, sudden overreaction, or distrusting anger even when it carries useful information. Pause before acting on anger, and express it with clarity and care before it becomes harmful.
Ansuz means “god” or “divine being”, and is associated with speech, wisdom, and inspired communication.

Ansuz often points to what is becoming clear through words, silence, advice, or sudden insight. It may also point to the need for honest expression, so that wisdom is not only received but given voice.
In relationships, Ansuz may point to the honesty of what is spoken and the care with which it is heard. An important conversation may need space for both people to speak honestly and be understood.
For purpose, Ansuz may point to messages that help clarify your path. Pay attention to what comes through signs, intuition, or meaningful conversations.
For security, Ansuz may point to the need for clear information before a decision feels safe. Facts, terms, expectations, or warnings may need to be understood before moving forward.
For the self, Ansuz may point to your relationship with your inner voice. Listen carefully to what you think and feel, and speak to yourself with greater honesty and clarity.
When reversed, Ansuz may point to miscommunication, misinformation, or poor advice. Be careful with what you accept as true, what guidance you follow, and what messages you pass on to others.

In relationships, Ansuz reversed may point to broken communication. This can show up as misunderstandings, outside advice being given too much power, or weaponised words. Clarify what was meant before reacting. Bring the conversation back to the people involved. Face the issue with honest, vulnerable dialogue instead of turning language into punishment.

For purpose, Ansuz reversed may point to a path being shaped by voices that are not truly your own. Separate genuine inner guidance from outside expectations, the need to prove yourself, or fear that sounds like practicality.

For the self, Ansuz reversed may point to fear, shame, or old criticism being mistaken for truth. Harsh words you’ve absorbed from others may still sound like your own inner voice. Check whether the story you are telling yourself is accurate before letting it define who you are.
Raidho is associated with riding, travel, and the ordered movement of a journey.
Raidho can point to the path you are on and the rhythm of your movement. Your route, pace, or timing may feel ordered and aligned, or may need adjustment.
In relationships, Raidho may point to the journey you share with another person. Look at whether both people are moving in the same rhythm and direction.
For purpose, Raidho may point to the direction your efforts are taking. Look at whether the way you are working is turning movement into steady, meaningful progress.
For the self, Raidho may point to navigating life in a way that is true to yourself. Look at whether your priorities, attention, and effort align with your values.

When reversed, Raidho may point to delays, disruption, or misaligned direction. Do not force movement; pause to check whether the path is still aligned. Choose your next step deliberately instead of rushing back into motion.

In relationships, Raidho reversed may point to a loss of shared direction. Each person may be expecting something different from the relationship. It may also be continuing from momentum rather than genuine alignment.

For purpose, Raidho reversed may point to movement that no longer has meaning behind it. Being busy, productive, or constantly progressing does not mean the path is still right for you. Choose your next step by asking what still feels purposeful, not what simply keeps things moving.

For the self, Raidho reversed may point to feeling off track or stuck in old patterns. You may be moving on autopilot, following a path that no longer fits, or repeating familiar habits that keep producing the same problems. Pause, look at where this keeps leading you, and choose one different step forward.
Kenaz is often associated with the torch, symbolizing light, knowledge, and illumination.
With Kenaz, something may be ready to come into clearer view. Insight, skill, or creativity may help you understand what was hidden and shape it into something useful.
In relationships, Kenaz often signifies a breakthrough in understanding. This might come through honesty, curiosity, or simply seeing each other with fresh eyes — all of which can deepen the bond.
For purpose, Kenaz points to the skills, ideas, or insights that illuminate your path. Once they come into view, put that understanding to work, both creatively and practically.
For the self, Kenaz points to clearer self-understanding. Something within you may be ready to be recognised, expressed, or shaped into form.

When reversed, Kenaz may point to lack of clarity or loss of inspiration. Something may be hidden, misunderstood, or being avoided. Slow down, reduce the noise around you, then face what begins to come into view.

In relationships, Kenaz reversed may point to something important being avoided. Misunderstanding can persist when an uncomfortable truth is being left unsaid. Avoidance may feel safer, but clarity gives the relationship a better chance to develop honestly.

For purpose, Kenaz reversed may point to a creative block or unclear direction. Pressure, fear of judgment, overload, or attachment to a stale idea may be blocking your creativity. Direction can become clearer when you face what no longer fits and allow your work to change.

For the self, Kenaz reversed may point to self-deception or difficulty accessing your own inner truth. You may be protecting an old self-image that no longer fits, or dismissing inconvenient doubts. Fear, shame, or outside noise may be making it harder to recognise what honestly matters to you.
Gebo means “gift”, symbolizing exchange, generosity, and the bond between giver and receiver.

Gebo points to the quality of exchange: what is freely offered, what is received, and what kind of bond is formed. Generosity can strengthen a bond when it does not become pressure, obligation, or imbalance.
For purpose, Gebo highlights the gifts you bring through your talents and effort. Look at whether what you offer is part of an exchange that feels meaningful and fair.
For the self, Gebo speaks to the balance between caring for others and tending to yourself. Allow yourself to receive support without feeling that you must earn it.
Wunjo means “joy” or “pleasure”, symbolizing harmony, satisfaction, and shared well-being.

Wunjo often reflects the kind of joy that comes from harmony within yourself and with others. Recognise what genuinely fulfils you, and let satisfaction be received without guilt or constant striving.
For purpose, Wunjo points to work that brings a sense of fulfilment. Meaningful work should offer joy, satisfaction, or genuine engagement, not only productivity.
For the self, Wunjo speaks to the joy that comes from accepting yourself and allowing happiness without needing outside validation.

When reversed, Wunjo may point to blocked joy or disharmony. Joy may have become conditional on outside circumstances, or difficult to receive unless it feels earned. There may also be a misalignment within you or around you that creates dissatisfaction or sorrow.

In relationships, Wunjo reversed may point to joy fading when disappointment or unmet needs go unaddressed. Joy may have also become conditional, depending too much on the other person or on unrealistic expectations. Question whether your expectations are fair and realistic, then bring true unmet needs into honest conversation.

For purpose, Wunjo reversed may point to progress that no longer feels fulfilling. You may be achieving goals and meeting expectations but lacking genuine satisfaction. Ask what would genuinely fulfil you, then recalibrate your goals around that rather than achievement alone.

For the self, Wunjo reversed may point to difficulty allowing yourself to feel joy. Happiness may feel undeserved, unsafe, or only acceptable after you have earned it. Let joy be something you are allowed to receive, not only something you must justify through progress or approval.
Hagalaz means “hail”, symbolizing disruption, sudden change, and forces beyond your control.
Hagalaz often appears when something has been shaken loose by events you cannot fully manage. Stop forcing control, protect what can be protected, and let clarity come after the storm passes.
In relationships, Hagalaz signals a disruption that calls for honest reassessment. Do not force harmony too quickly; let things settle first so the relationship can be seen more clearly.
For purpose, Hagalaz marks a disruption that shakes loose a path or plan you were trying to hold together. Look at how this change is reshaping your sense of meaning and what feels important now.
For security, Hagalaz signals a disruption that tests the structures you rely on for safety. See what has been exposed, and what needs to be strengthened once the storm has passed.
For the self, Hagalaz reflects a disruption that unsettles your self-image. A deeper understanding of who you are can emerge when the old image no longer holds.

Although Hagalaz may look different when inverted, it is generally considered to have no separate reversed meaning. Upright or reversed, Hagalaz often appears when something has been shaken loose by events you cannot fully manage. It may ask you to stop forcing control, protect what can be protected, and notice what becomes clearer once the storm has passed.
Nauthiz means “need” or “necessity”, pointing to the pressure that arises when something essential is lacking.
Nauthiz speaks to limitation or scarcity that reveals what is truly needed. Limitation can show what is essential and deepen your appreciation for what gives life real meaning.

For purpose, Nauthiz highlights unmet needs created by work or a path that no longer fits. You may have mistaken obligation or survival for purpose, and those needs can point toward a more fulfilling direction.
For security, Nauthiz highlights pressure around money, home, or resources you have relied on for safety. Reassess whether that pressure reveals a real need or a misplaced source of security.
For the self, Nauthiz highlights needs you have ignored or judged as weakness. You may have been focused on what seemed necessary while ignoring what you truly need.

Although Nauthiz may look different when inverted, it is generally considered to have no separate reversed meaning. Upright or reversed, Nauthiz can point to need, limitation, and the pressure that forces growth. It may invite you to examine what you truly require, to find resilience in constraint, and to discover the quiet strength that comes from enduring what feels difficult or restrictive.
Isa means “ice”, symbolizing stillness, preservation, and the slowing of movement or change.
Isa marks a pause where movement slows enough for clarity to form. This is an invitation to slow down, focus, and find peace in stillness.
In relationships, Isa calls for restraint before reacting impulsively or forcing a resolution. Let emotions settle before making a decision.
For purpose, Isa signals a pause in forward movement. Preserve your energy and clarify your direction before continuing.
For security, Isa signals a need for preservation rather than expansion. When resources are limited or stability is fragile, protecting what you have may be wiser than taking unnecessary risks.
For the self, Isa signals the need for inner stillness. Return to yourself and be present with what is here now.
Jera means “year” or “harvest”, symbolizing natural cycles, right timing, and patient effort.
Jera often points to results that cannot be rushed, only tended. Steady effort bears fruit when it works with the timing of the cycle rather than against it.
In relationships, Jera reflects the harvest of repeated patterns, not only one recent moment. What has been tended over time will show, and what has been neglected will show too.
For purpose, Jera reflects the season your work is in. Some seasons call for patience and tending. Others bring results that help you see whether this path is still worth cultivating.
For security, Jera highlights the season your finances or material resources are in. Some seasons call for investment and growth; others call for harvesting what has matured before committing more.

For the self, Jera reflects personal growth as a cycle of effort, harvest, reassessment, and recalibration. Growth depends not only on steady effort, but on seeing what that effort produces and adjusting what you continue to nurture.
Eihwaz means “yew tree”, symbolizing endurance, protection, and the deep connection between life and death.
Eihwaz can point to the endurance needed to move through difficult transitions or uncertainty. It is about staying rooted while life changes around you.

In relationships, Eihwaz speaks to bonds changing form over time. Some relationships may be fading, some strengthening, and others evolving into something different. Give attention and care to the bonds that can endure through change.

For purpose, Eihwaz speaks to a more enduring path that comes from staying rooted in your deeper self. Look at whether the direction you are pursuing reflects your values, inner truth, and the life you are trying to grow from within.
For security, Eihwaz speaks to protection that comes from deep roots rather than rigid defence. Build the habits, supports, and reserves that keep you steady through change.
For the self, Eihwaz speaks to staying rooted in who you are at your core through change. Growth and transformation do not require you to lose yourself.
Perthro is often linked to a dice cup, symbolizing chance, mystery, and unknown outcomes.
Perthro often appears where the outcome is not yet visible, and control can only go so far. Stay open to what has not yet been revealed, without trying to force certainty too soon.
In relationships, Perthro speaks to uncertainty about where a bond is leading. Become more comfortable with not fully knowing the relationship’s course, and stay open instead of trying to control it.

For purpose, Perthro is a reminder that meaning is often discovered through risk, experimentation, and stepping into the unknown. Stay curious and try different paths; experimentation may be how your purpose begins to reveal itself.

For the self, Perthro speaks to parts of you that are still hidden or unfolding. Not everything within you needs to be understood immediately; some self-knowledge reveals itself through lived experience.

When reversed, Perthro often reflects hidden information or discomfort with uncertainty. Avoid jumping to conclusions while key information is still missing. Release the need for a specific outcome, and stay open to what the unknown may reveal.

In relationships, Perthro reversed suggests that you may not have the full story. Avoid assuming motives before intentions, feelings, or unspoken truths become clear. Let the situation reveal itself in its own time.

For purpose, Perthro reversed suggests that the path has not fully revealed itself yet. Do not mistake uncertainty for failure or lack of direction. Stay open to unexpected possibilities instead of forcing your purpose to fit a specific outcome.

For the self, Perthro reversed suggests discomfort with parts of yourself that are still unknown. Avoid forcing a fixed answer about who you are before the full picture has emerged. Give yourself room to change and understand yourself more fully over time.
Algiz is often linked to the elk, symbolizing protection, defense, and alertness.
Algiz can point to protection without fear or withdrawal. It may ask you to notice your supports, strengthen your boundaries, and stay alert to what feels safe or unsafe.
In relationships, Algiz may point to the need for boundaries that protect connection. Healthy boundaries help preserve both your energy and the quality of your connections.
For purpose, Algiz may point to the need to protect your energy and focus. Notice what drains you, and what is worth receiving your time, attention, and effort.
For security, Algiz may point to warning signs that deserve your attention before they become larger problems. Strengthen your position early, so your stability is protected before pressure builds.

For the self, Algiz is a call to trust your intuition and stay alert to your inner signals. Notice what your body and instincts are telling you about where you feel safe, where you feel exposed, and where stronger boundaries are needed.

When reversed, Algiz may point to weakened protection, a false sense of security, or disconnection from your protective instincts. Take your warning signals seriously, and strengthen the boundaries or safeguards that help protect you.

In relationships, Algiz reversed may point to closeness being mistaken for safety. Hope, attachment, or familiarity may blur the difference between feeling close and being safe. Let their actions, not your attachment, decide how much access they are given.

For purpose, Algiz reversed may point to a path that exposes you to more harm than you are recognising. A goal may feel important, but that does not mean it is protecting your wellbeing. Strengthen the safeguards around your time, energy, and direction before giving more of yourself to it.

For the self, Algiz reversed may point to dismissing your own warning signals. You may be overriding discomfort, minimising unease, or talking yourself out of what your instincts are trying to show you. Rebuild self-trust by taking your protective responses seriously before they become louder.
Sowilo means “sun”, symbolizing vitality, guidance, and its life-giving energy.
Sowilo can point to life-giving energy and the strength it restores. It may ask you to move toward what renews you, rather than what burns through you.
In relationships, Sowilo may point to connections that feel life-giving rather than draining. Notice who brings warmth, clarity, and renewed energy into your life.
For purpose, Sowilo may point to work or direction that energises you and makes you feel alive. Focus on that vitality more than status, wealth, or external validation.
For the self, Sowilo may point to reconnecting with your natural energy and confidence. Notice what makes you feel alive, and let that part of yourself be expressed more fully.
Tiwaz is named after the god Tyr, symbolizing justice, courage, honour, and principled sacrifice.

Tiwaz can point to the courage to act from principle, especially when the easier path would compromise what matters. It may ask you to choose fairness over convenience, and to accept the cost of standing by your values.

In relationships, Tiwaz may point to the courage to act with integrity when avoidance would be easier. This can mean telling the truth, taking responsibility, or choosing fairness even when doing so may cost you the relationship itself.

For purpose, Tiwaz may point to work or direction that feels meaningful because it is rooted in integrity. A path is easier to stand behind when it reflects your deeper values, not only ambition, approval, or convenience.

For security, Tiwaz may point to integrity as a foundation for lasting stability. Acting fairly and honourably can build trust, strengthen your reputation, and create support that is stronger than money or control alone.
For the self, Tiwaz may point to the integrity of living by your deeper values. The values you choose to honour shape the person you become.

When reversed, Tiwaz may point to injustice or dishonour. Notice what you are accepting; unfairness can become easier to excuse when you are used to enduring it. Take a closer look at what you stand behind; loyalty, sacrifice, or conflict becomes dishonourable when it works against your values.

In relationships, Tiwaz reversed may point to unfairness being normalised. Unfairness may become easier to excuse when preserving the relationship matters more than facing what is wrong. Examine why you have endured the imbalance, then make clear what must change for the relationship to become fair.

For purpose, Tiwaz reversed may point to a worthy goal being pursued through the wrong means. The goal itself may be noble, but you may have chosen to pursue it in a way that betrays your values. Decide what you will no longer do for the goal, then find a way forward that still honours your values.

For security, Tiwaz reversed may point to accepting an unfair arrangement because challenging it could threaten your stability. You may be enduring conditions around work, money, housing, or family obligations because pushing back feels unsafe. Find small steps to reduce your dependence on the arrangement, so you can eventually challenge it from a safer position.

For the self, Tiwaz reversed may point to self-betrayal. You may be tolerating unfair treatment, trying to prove yourself where you are not respected, or staying silent when something feels wrong. Choose one act of self-respect: refuse what diminishes you, speak where you have stayed silent, or stop proving yourself to people who dismiss your worth.
Berkano is linked to the birch tree, symbolizing birth, growth, nurturing, and new beginnings.
Berkano can point to something new or tender that needs both care and protection. It may ask you to offer patience and trust the natural rhythm of growth and healing.
In relationships, Berkano may point to something tender that is still growing between people. Give it care, patience, and emotional safety so it has the right conditions to develop.
For purpose, Berkano may point to new possibilities that are not fully formed yet. Stay attentive to interests, ideas, or opportunities that may grow into something meaningful with the right support.
For security, Berkano may point to seeds of stability that are still taking root. Recognise what could grow into strong foundations, then protect and tend it with care.

For the self, Berkano is a reminder of the importance of self-nurture. Create conditions in your life that prioritise care, rest, and emotional support. Berkano is also linked to healing, and may ask you to recognise old wounds that need attention before growth can continue.

When reversed, Berkano may point to blocked growth or a fragile beginning. Look for what may be preventing progress: neglect, emotional blockage, unsafe conditions, or pressure. Do not underestimate what is still fragile; with enough care and time, it may grow into something valuable.

In relationships, Berkano reversed may point to a bond that is not being properly nurtured. Growth may be blocked by neglect, emotional withdrawal, pressure, or conditions that do not feel safe enough for vulnerability. Give the relationship the care it needs before expecting it to deepen.

For purpose, Berkano reversed may point to judging a new path too early because it has not produced visible results yet. A purpose may need quiet development before it can prove its value. Protect the early stage instead of forcing it to justify itself too soon.

For security, Berkano reversed may point to stability being weakened by neglected basic needs. Rest, health, home care, money management, or daily routines may need attention before they become harder to fix.

For the self, Berkano reversed may point to self-neglect or blocked inner growth. You may be pressuring yourself to heal, change, or become stronger before you have given yourself enough care. Give yourself the rest, safety, and support needed for growth before judging yourself for not changing faster.
Ehwaz means “horse”, symbolizing trust, movement, and harmonious cooperation.

Ehwaz can point to movement built on trust, like horse and rider working as one. It may ask you to nurture relationships that move in harmony, and to build connections based on mutual respect and shared direction.

In relationships, Ehwaz highlights the importance of true partnership. Mutual support and equal contribution help build trust, respect, and loyalty. It may also be a call to adapt to each other’s needs and find compromise where parts of your lives are not fully in sync.
For purpose, Ehwaz may point to progress that comes through partnership rather than solitary effort. The right collaborators or mentors can help clarify your direction and support your growth.
For security, Ehwaz may point to the limits of relying only on independence. Are you open to help, alliances, or partnerships that could build a more robust support network?

For the self, Ehwaz is an invitation to integrate all aspects of yourself, including the parts you may repress out of shame or fear. Wholeness comes from learning how these parts can be understood and brought into cooperation and harmony.

When reversed, Ehwaz may point to disharmony in partnership. Trust may have weakened, or there may be poor cooperation. Speak openly with the other side to understand what has caused the misalignment.

For purpose, Ehwaz reversed may point to progress being blocked because the path depends on cooperation that is not fully working. Support may be missing, priorities may differ, or the pace may be rushed. Clarify who is responsible for what, check whether everyone is still aiming for the same goal, and identify what support is missing. Then adjust the plan accordingly.

For the self, Ehwaz reversed may point to inner disharmony or resistance to integrating different parts of yourself. Your needs, instincts, or emotions may be pulling in different directions, making it harder to move forward. Understand the resistance before deciding whether to move forward or change direction.
Mannaz means “human” or “humankind”, symbolizing the self, community, and our shared human nature.

Drawing Mannaz can point to self-awareness, community, and the human connections that shape us. It may invite you to reflect on how you relate to yourself and others, to find balance between individuality and belonging, and to engage with the world from a place of conscious presence.

In relationships, Mannaz may point to the shared humanity between you and others. Meeting people with empathy and humility can deepen mutual understanding. Your role among others matters too; the way you show up can strengthen or weaken the community around you.
For purpose, Mannaz may point to the role your work plays within a wider community. Meaning can deepen when your work helps meet real human needs.
For security, Mannaz may highlight the importance of community and belonging. Nurture the communities around you; they can become a foundation for both practical help and moral support.

For the self, Mannaz may point to the way you come to know yourself through others. Much of your identity is shaped through shared human experience. What you notice in other people can reveal your own needs, patterns, strengths, and limitations.

When reversed, Mannaz may point to isolation or self-deception. Look at what is keeping you apart from others, whether it is fear, shame, mistrust, or pride. Ask what truth you may be avoiding because it threatens your comfort or ego.

In relationships, Mannaz reversed may point to seeing another person through your own distortions. You may be projecting insecurity, pride, or old wounds onto them, making it harder to recognise what is actually happening between you. Let honest feedback challenge the version of the story that only protects your ego.

For purpose, Mannaz reversed may point to disconnection from community or ego-driven motivation in your work. Your work may be centred more on status, recognition, or self-importance than on the people it is meant to serve. Refocus on who your work serves, not only the image it gives you.

For the self, Mannaz reversed may point to a distorted self-image. You may be seeing yourself through shame, pride, fear, or defensiveness rather than honesty. Let a fuller truth include both what you need to take responsibility for and what you no longer need to punish yourself for.
Laguz means “water” or “lake”, symbolizing flow, emotion, intuition, and hidden depths.
Laguz can point to emotions and intuitions moving beneath the surface. It may ask you to listen to what you feel and sense, rather than forcing everything into rigid plans.
In relationships, Laguz may point to emotions moving beneath the surface. Pay attention to what is felt but not fully spoken, and let empathy guide how you respond.
For purpose, Laguz may point to the importance of intuition in guiding you toward a path better aligned with your true self. Search deeper within for what resonates and what feels meaningful.
For security, Laguz may point to the importance of emotional safety. Notice what your inner signals reveal about where you feel at ease, where you feel unsettled, and what needs to change.
For the self, Laguz may point to the emotional depths within you. Pay attention to dreams, instincts, and subtle feelings; they may reveal parts of yourself that logic alone cannot reach.

When reversed, Laguz may point to emotional blockage or disconnection from intuition. Reflect on why you may be avoiding certain feelings, and look more closely at decisions where an inner signal is telling you something is not right.

In relationships, Laguz reversed may point to unspoken feelings making it unclear where the relationship truly stands. One or both people may sense that something is wrong, but avoid bringing it into the open because the truth could change the relationship. First understand what the feeling is asking for, then decide what needs to be spoken, changed, or accepted.

For purpose, Laguz reversed may point to following a path that looks right on the surface but feels wrong underneath. You may be ignoring an inner signal because the direction looks practical, expected, or too far along to question. Identify what the inner signal is objecting to before committing more deeply to the path.

For security, Laguz reversed may point to ignoring unease because nothing is visibly wrong yet. A situation may look stable, but your instincts may be warning you that something needs closer attention. Investigate the feeling, and look for what may need attention beneath the surface.

For the self, Laguz reversed may point to feeling flooded by emotions you have not yet understood. When too many feelings are moving at once, it can become harder to know what you truly need. Slow down and separate what is fear, grief, desire, or intuition before acting.
Ingwaz is named after the god Ing, symbolizing fertility, potential, and quiet growth.
Ingwaz can point to potential that is still forming beneath the surface. It may ask you to honour quiet growth, trusting that not everything needs to be visible before it becomes real.
In relationships, Ingwaz may point to a deeper bond forming quietly beneath the surface. Let it develop naturally, and allow what is growing between you to emerge in its own time.
For purpose, Ingwaz may point to a period of creative or personal incubation. Stay close to the process and make quiet, steady progress so your potential can strengthen before it is ready to emerge.
For the self, Ingwaz may point to private growth that is not yet visible to others. Give your inner potential time to strengthen, so it can emerge from a place of readiness rather than pressure.
Dagaz means “day” or “dawn”, symbolizing clarity, awakening, and the shift from darkness into light.
Dagaz can point to a threshold where something is becoming clearer after a period of uncertainty. It may invite you to welcome the shift, seeing what is now possible in a new light.

In relationships, Dagaz may point to a breakthrough in understanding or a shift in dynamics after a period of confusion or tension. Let this new clarity change how you show up, what you expect, or what you choose next.

For purpose, Dagaz may point to a breakthrough after a period of uncertainty. This may come as new clarity about your direction, progress where things once felt stuck, or an opportunity that opens a new path. Let the breakthrough guide your next step, and be willing to leave behind an old direction that no longer fits.

For the self, Dagaz may point to a personal breakthrough, inner transformation, or the arrival of greater self-understanding. Embrace this new version of yourself, and leave behind what no longer fits who you are becoming.
Othala means “ancestral property” or “heritage”, symbolizing home, roots, belonging, and inheritance.
Othala can point to the roots that shape your sense of home and belonging. It may invite you to honour what has been passed down, while choosing what kind of inheritance you want to carry forward.

In relationships, Othala may point to what you have inherited from your family or culture, and how it shapes the way you relate to others today. Use that awareness to break patterns that cause harm, and to strengthen the ones that help love, trust, and belonging endure.
For purpose, Othala may point to the legacy your work is helping to build. Consider whether your path is rooted in values you want to carry forward and contributes to something that can outlast you.

For security, Othala may point to the stability that comes from roots, home, and belonging. Consider what kind of foundation you are building, not only materially but through identity, values, place, and community.

For the self, Othala may point to the parts of your identity shaped by ancestry, roots, and culture. Carry forward the inherited wisdom, traits, and values you want to embody. Release the outdated traditions, inherited fears, or limiting beliefs that no longer serve you.

When reversed, Othala may point to inherited burdens, exclusion, or rigid attachment to tradition. Examine what you have inherited that no longer needs to be carried. Redefine where real belonging, family, or home can be found. Compare what a tradition protects with what it costs.

In relationships, Othala reversed may point to confusing family, history, or shared identity with real belonging. You may be staying close because someone is family, repeating old relationship patterns, or accepting treatment that was normal in the past but still harms you. Choose relationships that feel like home because they are safe and mutual, not only because they are familiar.

For purpose, Othala reversed may point to a life shaped by inherited expectations. You may be pursuing something because it was valued by your family, culture, or community, even if it no longer fits who you are becoming. Keep what gives your life roots, but release what keeps your purpose bound to someone else’s idea of belonging.

For security, Othala reversed may point to relying on family, home, or inheritance for safety when they also carry a cost. What protects you may also come with obligations or conditions you did not freely choose. Keep what genuinely supports you, but build enough independence that safety does not require staying trapped.

For the self, Othala reversed may point to carrying an inherited identity that no longer fits. You may be defining yourself through family roles, old expectations, or beliefs about worth that were passed down to you. Keep what feels true, but release the parts of yourself you learned to carry only to belong.
